content: The investigation teams can optimize their efforts by visiting fewer locations, which saves both time and resources. For studies targeting specific groups (e.g., a particular age group), it may be more efficient and less biased to include all eligible individuals within a household, especially in small enumeration areas. If the survey focuses solely on school-aged children, schools or classrooms can serve as clusters. However, convenience sampling is not acceptable for verifying whether a country has achieved regional hepatitis B control goals in children. The level of precision required for estimates should be determined based on the expected prevalence, study objectives, and the public health actions that will be guided by the results. Pre-existing data or regional estimates can help define parameters for calculating the minimum sample size. For data collection, tasks should be clearly assigned to team members, typically including an interviewer, a laboratory technician or nurse, and a supervisor. The size and composition of field teams may vary depending on the sample size, area coverage, laboratory tests required, and available resources. A logistics supplier should be identified to manage the storage and shipment of blood specimens within the public health system or through partners. The data collection process should include selecting relevant questions based on study objectives, defining children and adults, and adding items specific to the sampling procedure used. For cluster surveys, this includes recording cluster and household numbers. The choice of data collection tools should consider the volume of data, available resources for devices and software, security issues, power access, field team computer literacy, and mobile data connectivity. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for antibody detection typically require no more than 50 µL of specimen, while antigen detection may need up to 100 µL. Enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) may require up to 100 µL, and instrument-based immunoassays may need up to 1 mL of serum or plasma. RDTs are commercially available for detecting hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg), anti-HCV, anti-HAV, and anti-HEV. The quality of evidence for using dried blood spot (DBS) specimens in serological and nucleic acid testing for HCV and HBV is rated as low to moderate. DBS should only be used when better-performing tests are not feasible, and results should only be returned to patients if the assays have been validated for DBS use. Blood specimens should be stored and transported separately from vaccines or medicines. Testing strategies must adhere to WHO guidelines for viral hepatitis. Currently, no in vitro diagnostics are validated for use with DBS specimens, and their use would be considered off-label. If oral fluid-based tests are used, protocols must be adapted to the manufacturer's instructions. Specimen processing, storage, and transport should follow specific guidelines. Venous whole blood should be used immediately, while serum and plasma require specific handling and storage conditions. Capillary whole blood and oral fluid specimens should also be processed immediately, following the recommended protocols. DBS specimens can be stored at 4°C for up to three months or at -20°C for longer periods, but their use must be validated by the assay manufacturer. For data analysis, double data entry is recommended to minimize errors. A descriptive analysis plan should be prepared to identify and clean implausible data, incorporating checks into the data entry process. The analysis plan should account for the sampling design and weights. Potential biases that may affect study results should be listed. Safety and monitoring protocols should address adverse events, which include any unintended signs, symptoms, or diseases associated with study procedures. Serious adverse events (SAEs) are rare in biomarker surveys, as the primary procedure involves blood specimen collection, which carries minimal risk. Linkage to care should be adapted to the local healthcare system, with plans for pre-counseling, counseling, and treatment for patients testing positive. Community engagement strategies should be outlined to prepare the field and provide feedback to the community. Informed consent procedures should include a simplified assent form for children, allowing them to agree to the questionnaire and blood collection. The expected benefits of the survey should be detailed, including plans to use the results to guide public health actions. The survey budget should account for field costs, in vitro diagnostics, and treatment for positive cases, with funding sources identified for all components. In countries with national health insurance covering treatment, the budget can note that treatment will be supported by the insurance system.
